title: Responsible ML Engineering
oneLiner: Build ML that people can trust: traceable, explainable, fair, safe, secure, private and lawful.

what.html:
Responsible ML engineering means designing, building and running ML systems so they don't cause harm, and so you can prove it. That covers being able to trace exactly how a decision was made, explain it, make sure it's fair to different groups, keep it safe and secure, protect people's privacy, and follow the law.

Everyday versionA good bank clerk can tell you exactly why your loan was refused, applies the same rules to everyone, keeps your file locked away, and keeps records good enough for an auditor to check years later.

why.html:
• Software failures have killed patients, destroyed rockets, lost $460M in 45 minutes and wrongly convicted hundreds of postal workers.
  • ML adds new harms: discrimination, manipulation, surveillance, misinformation.
  • Regulators increasingly require evidence of responsible practice.

how.title: How software hurts people
how.html: Real incidents (radiation overdoses, a rocket self-destructing, runaway trading, wrongful convictions) teach testing, validation, kill switches and auditability. ML can also harm through safety failures, manipulation, polarisation, job loss, surveillance and discrimination.

how.title: Principles of responsible AI
how.html: Guide the whole lifecycle with principles: versioning and reproducibility, explainability, fairness, safety, security and privacy, aligned with the law and the values of everyone affected.

how.title: Can you reconstruct a decision?
how.html: When a customer says a credit decision was unfair, you need to know which model version, code and data produced it, even with A/B tests and canaries running. Version data, code and models; track where data came from; fix seeds and record environments so results can be recreated.

how.title: Versioning big data
how.html: Five options: full copies, daily deltas, offsets in an append-only log, per-record history, or versioning the pipeline (raw data + code + config). Provenance answers "where did this come from, who changed it?"; lineage answers "what happened to this table?"

how.title: Explain the decision
how.html: A black box that just says "high risk" can't be challenged. A scorecard with points per factor can. Transparency: you can see how it works. Interpretability: the logic makes sense. Explainability: you can say why this person got this result.

how.title: Fairness
how.html: A hiring model trained on years of male-dominated hiring learned to penalise women. Bias comes from history, tainted labels, skewed samples, limited features, small minority samples and proxies (postcode can stand in for ethnicity). Measure outcomes by group, document models and data, and plan for incidents.

how.title: Safety, security, privacy
how.html: Safety: robustness (a sticker shouldn't hide a stop sign), monitoring and alignment (doing what we meant, not gaming a metric). Security: keep data and models confidential, untampered and available. Privacy: models can infer pregnancy, politics or health from harmless-looking data.

how.title: Rules around the world
how.html: The EU uses binding, risk-based law; the UK relies on sector regulators; the US is mostly state-by-state; China regulates algorithms, generative AI and deepfakes centrally; Japan prefers voluntary guidance; India is building governance frameworks.

demo.html: Step through how biased data produces a biased model, biased outcomes, and then even more biased data, and what breaks the loop.

example.html:
A loan-approval system. Every decision is logged with the model version, feature values and code commit. Applicants get a reason list from an interpretable scorecard. Approval rates are monitored by gender and region each week; when the disparate impact ratio for one region fell below 0.8, the team found a postcode proxy and removed it. Training data is versioned by pipeline (raw v3 + ETL v5 + config v2), the API is rate-limited against model stealing, and only the minimum personal data is stored.

Supplementary Different fairness metrics can conflict; choose one deliberately and record why.

misunderstandings: Removing gender and race columns makes a model fair.
Proxies carry the same information; measure outcomes.
People need reasons for their own decision.
Responsible AI is a legal checkbox at the end.
It's engineering practice across the whole lifecycle.
If data is anonymised, privacy is solved.
Models can re-infer sensitive attributes from other data.
takeaways: Learn from real software failures; ML adds harms like discrimination and manipulation.
Responsible AI principles: versioning/reproducibility, explainability, fairness, safety, security, privacy.
Version data, code and models; distinguish provenance from lineage; fix sources of nondeterminism.
Prefer interpretable models where decisions affect people; measure fairness by group and watch for proxies and feedback loops.
Safety = robustness, monitoring, alignment; security = CIA; privacy = control over personal information; regulation differs by region.
thirty: Software failures such as Therac-25, Ariane 5, Knight Capital and the Post Office Horizon scandal show the cost of untested, unauditable systems, and ML adds harms of safety, manipulation, polarisation, job loss, surveillance and discrimination. Responsible AI applies principles across the lifecycle. Versioning, provenance and reproducibility let you reconstruct any decision; large datasets are versioned through full copies, deltas, offsets, per-record history or pipeline versions, and provenance (origin and changes) is distinct from lineage (flow and transformations). Transparency, interpretability and explainability let people understand and challenge decisions. Fairness requires watching six sources of bias, including proxies, and feedback loops. Safety covers robustness, monitoring and alignment; security follows the CIA triad; privacy guards against sensitive inference. Regulation ranges from the EU's binding risk-based law to voluntary guidance.
